title: pkix-dane-resolver: standing obligation to track IANA root KSK rolls
description:
## Why this exists

PKIX-j32w.5 decided that pkix-dane-resolver ships the IANA DNSSEC root KSK compiled in as a crate constant, with a caller override. That buys zero-config DANE validation on every platform, including macOS and Windows which generally ship no trust-anchor file.

The accepted cost: when IANA rolls the root KSK, every build of the crate stops validating DNSSEC until a release carries the new key. Since DANE verdicts then become Bogus or Indeterminate, the PKIX-j32w.4 policy means opportunistic callers silently lose DANE and strict callers start failing connections outright. That is a security-relevant outage caused by the crate going stale, not by anything the consumer did.

## Why it is P2 rather than P3

The last root KSK roll was 2018 and the next is unscheduled, so nothing is due now. It is filed at P2 anyway because the failure mode is silent for opportunistic callers and total for strict ones, and because the obligation is easy to lose across years and maintainers — which is exactly how it will be lost if it sits at backlog priority.

## What this bead covers

1. The crate must document the obligation prominently — crate-level rustdoc and README, not a buried comment: which KSK is shipped, that a roll requires a crate release, and how to supply an anchor manually in the interim.
2. The shipped anchor should carry its key tag and a comment naming the IANA key it came from, so staleness is auditable by reading the source.
3. Decide and record how a roll gets noticed. IANA announces rolls well in advance; options include a documented maintainer checklist item, a CI check against IANA's published root-anchors XML, or a test that fails once a configured date passes. A CI check is the only option that does not depend on a human remembering.
4. Consider whether the crate should expose the OS trust-anchor file as an opt-in source (/var/lib/unbound/root.key, /etc/trusted-key.key) for deployments that would rather track distro updates than crate releases. PKIX-j32w.5 rejected file-first as the DEFAULT because of macOS and Windows; it was not rejected as an option.

## Acceptance

[ ] Obligation documented in crate-level rustdoc and README
[ ] Shipped anchor annotated with its key tag and IANA provenance
[ ] A mechanism for noticing a roll chosen and recorded, with a CI check preferred over a human checklist
[ ] Opt-in OS-anchor-file source considered and the outcome recorded
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-11-24. The obligation is now guarded by a scheduled CI check rather than by anyone remembering it.

## This bead named the wrong crate

It was filed while the decision stood that pkix-dane-resolver would compile the IANA root KSK in. That decision was reversed the same day, on Mark's point that pkix must not depend on the OS or the filesystem and that the key should be separately auditable and updatable: the anchors went into their own crate, pkix-dnssec-anchor, and pkix-dane-resolver ships no anchor at all and requires a caller-supplied one.

So the obligation lives in pkix-dnssec-anchor, and the reversal already bought most of what this bead wanted -- a roll is now a release of one tiny data crate that consumers pick up with cargo update, rather than a release of the resolver that they must wait for.

## What was actually missing

Of this bead's four items, two were already satisfied by the split and one was decided against:

1. Document the obligation -- partly done in the crate's rustdoc. The crate had NO README at all, while every other crate in the workspace has one, so a reader on crates.io saw none of it. Now written, and the rustdoc expanded.
2. Key tag and provenance in the shipped source -- already done by the generator: each anchor carries its IANA KeyDigest id, key tag and validity dates.
3. HOW A ROLL GETS NOTICED -- not done, and the only item that mattered. This is the work.
4. Expose the OS trust-anchor file as an opt-in source -- REJECTED, and recorded as rejected rather than left open. PKIX-j32w.5's amendment ruled out OS and filesystem access for trust material on principle, not merely on platform-coverage grounds. Revisiting it would reopen a decision made deliberately.

## The mechanism

gen.sh --check: fetch IANA's anchors, verify the detached PKCS#7 signature, report drift against the committed set, write nothing.

Three design points worth keeping:

- It compares id, key tag, algorithm, digest type, digest and validity rather than whole files. IANA reformats and rewrites the TrustAnchor id attribute without changing any anchor, so a byte comparison would cry wolf.
- It exits 2 rather than 1 when the signature fails to verify. That is NOT a key roll: it means the fetch was tampered with or ICANN's signing certificate changed, and either wants investigating before anything is regenerated. Conflating the two would invite regenerating from a bad fetch.
- It lives in gen.sh rather than a separate script, so the IANA URLs and the signature verification exist in exactly one place. A checker that drifted from the generator would be worse than no checker.

.github/workflows/iana-anchors.yml runs it monthly, plus on any pull request touching the crate so a regeneration is checked against IANA in the change that performs it.

Monthly rather than weekly or daily: a root KSK roll is announced well in advance and has happened once since 2010. A job that runs more often than the thing it watches mostly teaches people to ignore it. Separate from quality-gates.yml so an unrelated pull request does not fail because a third party published something -- that would be confusing and unactionable by whoever opened it.

## Verified, because a checker that only ever passes is untested

Doctored the committed XML to simulate IANA withdrawing the 2024 key, confirmed --check fails with a readable diff naming the changed field, then restored it and confirmed it passes. The preference in this bead for a CI check over a human checklist is therefore satisfied by something demonstrated to fire.

## Acceptance

[x] Obligation documented in crate-level rustdoc AND a README -- the README did not previously exist
[x] Shipped anchors annotated with key tag and IANA provenance -- already the case, confirmed
[x] A mechanism for noticing a roll chosen and recorded, CI preferred over a human checklist -- gen.sh --check plus a monthly workflow, and verified to detect drift
[x] Opt-in OS-anchor-file source considered and the outcome recorded -- rejected, per the no-OS no-filesystem decision on PKIX-j32w.5

## Residual risk, stated plainly

The workflow has never run on GitHub. The script is verified locally and the YAML parses, but the Actions-specific parts are only exercised on the first push or scheduled firing. The same caveat applies to every workflow added today.
